lessons.notes: Unit 5 has a folk play 'The Swan and the Princes' (p. 1–4) set in Kapilavastu, and a poem 'Somebody’s Mother' (p. 17–19). The play is about Prince Siddhartha, who saved a swan, and Prince Devadatta, who shot it. Typos in the book: 'Siddharta/Siddharth/Sidharth' are spelt in different ways; the correct spelling is Siddhartha. 'solt' in the vowel task should be 'salt'. The ILA passage is read aloud by the teacher and is not printed in the book; its answers must be checked by the teacher against the passage.
ab: ILA – Listen to the passage and answer (p. 1)
1. What did each woman claim?
Each woman claimed that she was the real mother of the baby and so had the right to own and look after it.
2. What did the minister suggest?
The minister suggested that the baby be split in two, so that each woman would get half of the baby.
3. Why do you think the second woman offered the baby to the first woman, after she heard the minister?

4. How did the minister come to the correct conclusion? What was the reason for his judgement?

The minister tested the women with his suggestion. The second woman refused to divide the baby and offered it to the first woman, which showed that she loved the child; so the minister decided she was the real mother.
C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 5)
1. What was the complaint of Devadatta against Prince Siddhartha?
Devadatta complained that Prince Siddhartha had taken his swan, which he had shot, and refused to give it back.
2. Why did Siddhartha claim that the swan was his?
Siddhartha claimed the swan was his because he had saved its life.
3. How did the bird react to Devadatta’s call?
The swan trembled and cried with fear, and it would not go to Devadatta.
4. What did Siddhartha say to the swan? What did the bird do?
Siddhartha said, “Dear swan, don’t be afraid. I’ve come to you. Come and sit on my arms.” The swan at once flew onto his arms.
5. What made Devadatta and Siddhartha approach the King?
Devadatta went to the King to complain and seek justice, and the King then called Siddhartha to explain his side.
6. How did each of them defend their actions?
Devadatta said he had shot the swan, so it was his. Siddhartha said he had saved the swan’s life, and that a kshatriya cannot give up a suppliant.
7. How did the Chief Minister resolve the dispute in the end?
The Chief Minister asked each prince to call the swan. The swan refused to go to Devadatta and flew onto Siddhartha’s arms, so the King decided that the swan belonged to Siddhartha.
C2 – Put the following events in the order in which they occur in the play and write them in a paragraph (p. 5)

Events: 1. The swan flew onto Siddhartha’s arms. 2. Devadatta appealed to the King for justice. 3. Siddhartha nursed the bird with great care. 4. Devadatta called the swan to him. 5. Siddhartha called the swan lovingly. 6. Devadatta shot an arrow at the bird.

Devadatta shot an arrow at the bird. Siddhartha picked it up and nursed the bird with great care. Devadatta appealed to the King for justice. Devadatta called the swan to him, but the swan trembled with fear. Siddhartha then called the swan lovingly, and the swan flew onto his arms.
Order: 6 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5 → 1
C3 – Write an imaginary dialogue between the swan and Prince Siddhartha (p. 5)
Complete the dialogue (sample answer – answers will vary)

Swan: Dear Siddhartha, I want to talk to you.
Prince: Yes, my dear. What is it? Tell me, don’t fear anyone.
Swan: Dear prince, it is only because of your kindness that I am still alive today.
Prince: Why do you say that?
Swan: Imagine what would have happened to me if you had not saved me from Devadatta’s arrow.
Prince: Don’t you think it was my duty to help a creature in danger?
Swan: Yes, but your kindness is rare. I will always remember you.
Prince: Live happily and freely, my friend.

C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 20)
1. What kind of a woman do you find in this poem?
She is an old, poor and ragged woman, weak and alone, who is uncared for.
2. Where was the woman standing? Why was she standing there?
She was standing at the crossing of the street, waiting for a long time to cross the road.
3. Why was the woman very anxious?
She was anxious because the street was slippery and the carriage wheels and horses’ feet might crowd her down, and nobody came to help her.
4. What are the children compared to?
The children are compared to a flock of sheep.
5. Did the boys lend the old woman a helping hand?
No. Most of the boys passed her by; only the gayest boy of the group offered to help her.
6. Why was the old woman hesitating to cross the street?
She was hesitating because she was afraid that the carriage wheels or the horses’ feet would crowd her down in the slippery street.
C2 – Read and discuss your responses with your partner. Then write (p. 20)
1. How did the boy help the old woman?
He paused beside her and whispered that he would help her across. He guided her trembling feet along the street while she placed her aged hand on his strong young arm.
2. What made the boy happy?
He was happy because he had helped the old woman cross the street safely; his young heart was happy and well content.
3. What did the boy tell his friends?
He told his friends that she was somebody’s mother, and that someone should lend a hand to help their own mothers when they are poor and grey.
4. What did the old woman say in her prayers that night? Why?
She prayed, “God be kind to the noble boy who is somebody’s son and pride and joy”, because he had helped her when no one else did.
5. Do you like this poem? Why or why not?

C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 37)
1. What sort of sounds can one hear early in the morning?
The sounds of the waking sea and wind, the call of the sea gull and the call of the fishermen to one another, ‘Rise, brothers, rise’.
2. How is the wind described in line two?
The wind is described as lying asleep in the arms of the dawn, like a child that has cried all night.
3. Why are the nets to be gathered?
The nets are gathered to capture the leaping wealth of the tide, that is, the fish.
4. What do you think is the wealth to the fishermen?
The fish caught from the sea is their wealth. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
C2 – Read and discuss your responses with your partner. Then write (p. 37)
1. What do you understand from the first line of the poem, ‘The wakening skies pray to the morning light’?
It means the sky is becoming bright at dawn, as if it is praying for the morning light to come.
2. The poet says, ‘Let us set our catamarans free.’ What does it mean?
It means the fishermen should take their boats out to the sea and start fishing.
3. What happens if the fishermen are late in starting their work?
They may miss the best time for catching fish, and the wealth of the tide may be lost. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
4. Why does the poet say: [a] the sea is our mother, [b] the cloud is our brother, [c] the waves are our comrades all?
Because the fishermen depend on the sea for their living, like a mother; they feel close to the clouds and the sea as brothers, and the waves work with them as friends and companions.
C3 – Answer the following in a paragraph (p. 38)
1. The poet describes many things as sweet. What are they? Among them, what is considered to be the sweetest?

Sweet things in the poem are the shade of the coconut glade, the scent of the mango grove, the sands at the full moon with the sound of the voices we love, and the kiss of the spray and the dance of the wild foam’s glee. The sweetest is ‘the kiss of the spray and the dance of the wild foam’s glee’, which the poet calls ‘sweeter’.

2. The wind lies asleep in the arms of the dawn like a child.

3. The sea is our mother.

4. The cloud is our brother.

Additional Reading – The Diver (p. 38–39)
1. Who is the speaker in the poem?
The speaker is a diver.
2. ‘A touch explode’ (line 5). What causes the explosion?
The bushes burst into shrimps when the diver touches them, which is why the poet says they ‘explode’.
3. The speaker says of ‘those pearls’. What really are these pearls?
The pearls are the bubbles of the diver’s breath; the speaker says ‘Those pearls were my breath!’
4. Why does the diver wish to come back to the surface?
The cold grips his flesh and limbs and he begins to shiver, so he is pulled back to the surface and swims to the beach.

ab: ILA – Your teacher reads a story. Listen and answer (p. 40)
1. Why did the king feel proud of himself?
He felt proud because his ministers told him he was the most handsome person in the world; he even said that he was more attractive than the gods.
2. Who felt angry with the king? Why?
The gods in heaven felt angry, because the king had claimed to be more attractive than them. They wanted to teach him a lesson.
3. How did the tree come to know about the king’s horns?
The king himself told the tree that he had two horns on his head. The tree later fell, and its wood made drums that repeated the words.
4. The ministers praised the king. Which phrase is used to mean ‘praised’?
‘Compliments’ (‘Impressed by their compliments’).

C4 – Read and discuss with your partner. Then write (p. 50–51)
1. Why was the Emperor not able to give much time to the business of his kingdom?
He spent so many hours every day in his dressing room trying out new clothes that he had very little time for the affairs of his kingdom.
2. Why did the Emperor want a new set of clothes every day?
He was very fond of new clothes and wanted a tailor who could make a different set every day.
3. What did the Chief Adviser tell the Emperor about the two weavers?
He said that two weavers from a distant place had been waiting outside the palace, claiming to be magic tailors who could make the most beautiful clothes.
4. What did the two weavers say about the magic way of making beautiful silk cloth?
They said the cloth is so finely woven, with rich colours and attractive patterns, that only a great Emperor can wear it; wise men can see it but fools cannot.
5. How would the clothes made of the magic cloth be different from the ordinary clothes that people wear?
Only wise men fit for their jobs could see the magic clothes; the clothes would be invisible to fools and to those unfit for their work, unlike ordinary clothes which everyone can see.
6. Why did the Emperor think that the weavers had given him an excellent idea?
By wearing a suit of their cloth he would get new clothes and also find out who was fit to manage the affairs of his kingdom.
7. What conditions did the weavers lay down for starting the work?
They needed a large quantity of the finest silk, the purest gold thread and several jewels, and a room in the palace.
8. How did the two weavers start their work on the two looms?
They pretended to work on the looms, having secretly put away the silk, gold thread and jewels in their bags.
9. Why was the Chief Adviser greatly surprised when he first saw them working?
He could not see any cloth or thread on the looms.
10. How did the weavers try to confuse the Chief Adviser?
They described circles, flowing lines and dark red and sky blue colours on a gold background, which did not exist.
11. What made the Chief Adviser feel worried about his own fitness for the post he was holding?
The weavers had said that fools and those unfit for their jobs cannot see the clothes, so he feared he was a fool and unfit for his post.
12. What was the terrible experience of the Adviser’s Special Assistant?
He could not see any cloth on the looms, and he feared that he himself might be a fool or unfit for the job, so he kept the secret to himself.
13. How did the two weavers pretend to make the Emperor’s new clothes and help him wear them?
They pretended to hand over the coat and trousers and helped the Emperor to ‘wear’ the invisible clothes in the dressing room.
14. Why did the Chief Adviser request the Emperor to show himself on the balcony?
The people were waiting outside to see the Emperor in his new clothes before the procession.
15. What was the Emperor’s reply to his request?
He said, ‘Certainly, certainly’ and that he would come as soon as he was ready.
16. How did the courtiers behave when the Emperor walked towards the balcony almost naked?
They showed surprise but said nothing, because they had been told that only wise men could see the clothes.
17. What happened when the Emperor reached the balcony?
The cheers stopped suddenly and there was pin-drop silence; then a little child laughed and said that the Emperor had no clothes on at all.

1. Describe the Emperor’s character. He is proud and foolish, but he has another weakness shown in his behaviour towards his Chief Adviser.

* Manoj replied that he would come the next day. (ಮಾದರಿ – ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿಗಳ ಉತ್ತರ ಭಿನ್ನವಾಗಿರಬಹುದು)
C. Reading – Man – The enemy: Task 1 (p. 56)
Make a list of the animals mentioned above and the use for which they are killed.
Baby seals – for their skins; Crocodiles – skins used for hand bags and shoes; Elephants – ivory used for jewellery; Whales – for their oil.
C. Reading – Task 2: Inferential comprehension – facts about cats and dogs (p. 56–57)
Family
Cats: tigers; Dogs: wolves
Faithful to
Cats: their home area (not to a master); Dogs: their master
Hunting habits
Cats: hunt alone; Dogs: hunt in groups
Body language (in anger)
Cats arch their back and try to look large; dogs pull their lips back and show their teeth
Special skills
Cats can fall from a significant height and survive without much injury; dogs guard property and can sense any smell in no time
D. Grammar – Reported Speech: Task 1 – fill in the blanks using the clues (p. 57–58)

Clues: 1. that he was, but his father was dead; 2. not to worry; 3. if he should bring the stranger in; 4. to go and tell that to his mother; 5. if he was Mustafa’s son; 6. that he was his father’s brother; 7. that it was indeed a sad news.

Alladin met a stranger who asked him if he was Mustafa’s son. Alladin told him that he was, but his father was dead. The stranger consoled him saying not to worry and told him that it was indeed a sad news. He further informed him that he was his father’s brother and asked him to go and tell that to his mother. Alladin went and told his mother that there was a stranger at the door who said he was his uncle. He further asked her if he should bring the stranger in.
D. Grammar – Reported Speech: Task 2 (p. 58)
1. Kiran said to Reshma, “I’m enjoying my new job.”
Kiran told Reshma that she was enjoying her new job.
2. “Renu has invited us to the party,” said Reshma.
Reshma said that Renu had invited them to the party.
3. Kiran said, “We must attend the party. Let’s plan for it.”
Kiran said that they must attend the party and that they should plan for it.
4. Kiran’s father said, “You must visit your grandmother more often.”
Kiran’s father told him/her that he/she must visit the grandmother more often.
5. Reshma said, “We are planning to visit her coming Sunday.”
Reshma said that they were planning to visit her the following Sunday.
6. “Last month you were busy. So you dropped the idea,” said Kiran’s mother.
Kiran’s mother told her that she had been busy the previous month, so she had dropped the idea.
E. Writing – Punctuation: Task 2 – insert commas (p. 58)
1. Sir John Smith the Vice Chancellor arrived just now.
Sir John Smith, the Vice Chancellor, arrived just now.
2. As the teacher entered all the students stood up.
As the teacher entered, all the students stood up.
3. “John when will you come?” said Prema.
“John, when will you come?” said Prema.
4. Not knowing whom to address he kept silent.
Not knowing whom to address, he kept silent.
5. If you do not know the answer ask the teacher.
If you do not know the answer, ask the teacher.
E. Writing – Punctuation: Task 3 – apostrophe (p. 59)
Children’s Day; Teachers’ Day; men’s wear; women’s wear; ‘The Emperor’s New Clothes’; A Nation’s Strength

The apostrophe shows possession, usually with living beings. Children’s (plural, possessive ’s), Teachers’ (plural ending in s, possessive ’), men’s and women’s (irregular plurals with ’s). Titles of the play and the poem also show possession correctly.
E. Writing – Punctuation: Task 4 – apostrophe in paragraph (p. 59)
Use apostrophe wherever necessary in the paragraph.

Aristotle was born in Stagira, a Greek outpost on the Macedonian coast. His father was a doctor in the court of Philip II of Macedon. When Aristotle was about 17, he left for Athens where he became a pupil of Plato. He stayed in Plato’s Academy in Athens for 20 years, first as a student and later as a teacher. Then he was invited back to Macedon to tutor Alexander, Philip’s son. Aristotle’s enthusiasm for wisdom and for free expression of ideas greatly influenced the young prince, and clearly played a role in eventually making him Alexander the Great. Interestingly, Socrates’ disciple was Plato, Plato’s disciple was Aristotle, and Aristotle’s disciple was Alexander the Great.
IRA – Read what the Encyclopaedia says about a machine and answer (p. 60)
Name a few machines that we use. How do they run or work?

Examples: mixer – grinds food with a motor and blades; fan – electric motor turns the blades to move air; bicycle – pedals turn the wheel using a chain and gears; sewing machine – motor/pedal moves the needle to stitch cloth; pulley – lifts loads with a rope. (ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು)
Man has learnt how to sail on the seas, how to fly in the sky and how to reach the moon; but he has not yet learnt how to live on this earth. Do you agree?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Classify the words emu, cog, nut, wedge, bear, mouse, furnace, tool, boar, rhino, file, ray, turtle, mink into Mechanics and Biology.
Mechanics: cog, nut, wedge, furnace, tool, file, bear (ball-bearing), mouse (computer). Biology: emu, boar, rhino, ray, turtle, mink, bear (animal), mouse (animal). Used in both: bear, mouse.
C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 63)
1. Fill in the boxes with the steps of making a machine (first stanza).
1 mined; 2 melted; 3 cast; 4 wrought; 5 hammered; 6 cut; 7 filed; 8 tooled; 9 gauged
2. What do simple machines need to start working?
Some water, coal and oil, and a thousandth of an inch to give them play (a little space to move).
3. Name at least five machines and write how they are useful to man.
e.g. an iron box – for ironing clothes; a fan – for cooling; a mixer – for grinding; a sewing machine – for stitching clothes; a bicycle – for transport. (ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು)
4. What can a machine not do? (stanza 4)
A machine cannot comprehend a lie, and it can neither love, pity nor forgive.
5. What is the risk, if the machine is mishandled? (stanza 4)
If a slip is made in handling the machine, the person may die.
C2 – Read and discuss with your partner. Then write (p. 63–64)
1. How are machines and human beings different? Study the last stanza.
Machines cannot love, pity or forgive, nor comprehend a lie, but humans can. Machines are only children of the human brain, although they have great power, weight and size.
2. Do you observe any rhyme scheme in each stanza? Write the rhyming words.
Stanza 1: mine – design; pit – fit. Stanza 2: ask – task; play – day. Stanza 3: drive – dive; light – write. Stanza 4: lie – die; forgive – live. Stanza 5: again – brain.
3. List all the words that suggest motion.

taken, melted, cast, hammered, cut, filed, pull, haul, push, lift, drive, print, plough, weave, heat, light, run, jump, swim, fly, dive, see, hear, count, read, write (ಮುಖ್ಯ ಚಲನೆ: pull, haul, push, lift, drive, run, jump, swim, fly, dive)
4. Note how the word ‘and’ is used in the poem. Identify other repeated words and phrases. What is the effect of repetition?

‘And’ is used many times in a list (polysyndeton), and phrases like ‘We were’, ‘We can’ and ‘We are’ are repeated. This shows the machine’s long list of abilities and gives the poem a steady, rhythmic effect, emphasising the machine’s strength.
Additional Reading – Million Million Years Later (V.G. Bhatta) (p. 64)
Do you find anything common between this poem and the poem ‘Machine’? Discuss in the class.

Both poems speak of man’s power and his own creations, and both warn that human actions can lead to destruction (machines and humans can be dangerous if misused). ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

lessons.au: Daniel Miller (Prose, Britannica-based); Clifford Henry Dyment (Poem)

lessons.notes: Unit 8 has a prose text 'Luther Burbank' (p. 65–69, based on Britannica) and a poem 'The Axe in the Wood' by Clifford Henry Dyment (p. 76–79). The IRA photo of Haji Kalimullah Khan (p. 65) is optional for the questions (answers come from the text). Book errors to correct: V1 vocabulary list has 'thorn less' (write 'thornless'); in Listen and Speak, 'load' and 'tone' are /əʊ/ (not /aʊ/); in the news story the questions 'troubling (P6)' refer to a paragraph that is not in the text (only 5 paragraphs); the Supplementary Reader lists ‘Lal Bahadur Sastry’ but the lesson is spelt ‘Shastry’ in the text; Wordsworth poem ‘pagon’ should be ‘pagan’. ab: ILA – Your teacher reads a story. Listen and answer (p. 65)
1. Name any one trick which the magician says he can perform.
He said he can make a lunch box disappear within a second, and change a piece of paper into a hundred rupee note.
2. Usually how does a magician play a trick?
He hypnotizes people, that is, he captures their attention.
3. Do you think a magician can grow many kinds of mangoes on a single tree?
No. A magician cannot grow 100 kinds of mangoes on a single tree; he said, ‘Sorry, that I can’t.’ Luther Burbank can do such things.
IRA – Read the following and answer the questions (p. 65)
1. What is Haji Kalimullah Khan’s main achievement?
He has grown 300 different kinds of mangoes on a single tree (from Mallihabad, U.P.).
images/class-8/english/c8-en-l08-khan-photo.webp
2. How has the Government recognised his achievement?
He has been awarded the Padmashri award, and his name is in the Limca Book of Records.
3. Which words are used to mean: 1. greatly 2. unbelievable event 3. of late 4. kinds 5. technique
1. immensely; 2. mystery (miracle); 3. recently; 4. varieties; 5. craft
C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 69)
1. Name the fields in which Luther Burbank’s influence prevails.
Agriculture, horticulture, forestry and livestock.
2. When was Luther Burbank born?
On March 7, 1849.
3. What was Luther Burbank’s goal in life?
To grow and graft new varieties of fruits, vegetables and plants.
4. Name the book that helped Burbank to decide on his goal of life.
Darwin’s ‘Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication’.
5. Mention the name of the new variety of potato plant grown by Burbank.
The Idaho Potato.
6. How was the weather in the State of California?
The weather was mild and the soil was rich and varied.
7. How many varieties of fruits did Burbank grow on an acre of his farm?
Several thousand different varieties of fruits.
8. What is grafting?
Grafting is taking a twig or piece of living material from one plant and joining it to another plant so that it grows on it.
C2 – Tick (√) the true statements and (×) the others (p. 70)
a) growing hundreds of varieties of apples
b) spending 15 years for a tree to bear fruit
c) making a young plant yield fruit in a year or two
d) growing about 526 varieties of apples in an acre of his farm
×  (526 varieties were grown on one tree, not on an acre)
C3 – Read and discuss with your partner. Then write (p. 70)
1. How did Burbank’s genius benefit the life of the common man?
His new varieties of fruits, vegetables and flowers, such as the Idaho potato and improved cherries and blackberries, improved the food and life of ordinary people.
2. Why did Burbank move from Massachusetts to California?
The climate of his native place was not suitable for his work, whereas California had a mild weather and rich soil.
3. What did Burbank call his new home? Why?
He called it ‘The chosen spot’ of all this earth, because nature there was most suited to his work.
4. How did grafting help Burbank in his experimentation?
Grafting twigs of young plants on fruit-bearing trees helped him get fruit in two or three years instead of fifteen, and grow many varieties on one tree.
5. In what way did Burbank save space and speed up his experiments?
By grafting many twigs on a single tree, he grew several varieties on one tree, which saved space and sped up his experiments.
6. What were Burbank’s experiments on cherry, blackberry, cactus and Shasta Daisy?
He developed an improved cherry, a thornless blackberry, a cactus without thorns used as livestock food, and the Shasta Daisy flower.
C4 – Write a paragraph on each of the following (p. 70)
1. Write a note on Burbank’s early life.

Luther Burbank was born on March 7, 1849 and brought up on a farm in Massachusetts. He was attracted to the wonders of nature and learned the techniques of growing crops and plants. After reading Darwin’s book, he decided to devote his life to growing new varieties of plants. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
2. Describe the three techniques on which Burbank’s experiments were based.

First, he collected domestic plants and brought in foreign varieties, growing them under different conditions. Secondly, he grew many varieties by changing water, food, temperature, light or space, and by crossing plants with dissimilar qualities. Thirdly, he recognised and selected the plants that showed desirable changes for further experiments.
3. How did Burbank react when some of his efforts ended in failure?
He was not disappointed; his devotion remained strong. For example, when a cross of tomato and potato had no commercial value, he continued his work with patience.
V1 – Collocations: fill in the blanks with suitable describing words from the box (p. 71)
Box: desert, commercial, successful, scientific, thornless, rich, white. 1. ____ community 2. ____ soil 3. ____ blackberry 4. ____ cactus 5. ____ attempt 6. ____ value
1. scientific community; 2. rich soil; 3. thornless blackberry (or white blackberry); 4. desert cactus (or thornless cactus); 5. successful attempt; 6. commercial value
V2 – Classify the names into fruits, vegetables and flowers (p. 71)
orange, plum, neem, desert cactus, mango, blackberry, banana, brinjal, potato, cherry, lemon, apple, grapes, jasmine, lotus, shasta daisy, marigold, rose, tomato, peach, watermelon, carrot

Fruits: orange, plum, mango, blackberry, banana, cherry, lemon, apple, grapes, peach, watermelon. Vegetables: brinjal, potato, tomato (commonly used as a vegetable), carrot. Flowers: jasmine, lotus, shasta daisy, marigold, rose. (Neem – a tree; desert cactus – a plant; ಈ ಎರಡನ್ನು ‘ಇತರೆ’ ಎಂದು ಇಡಬಹುದು)
A. Listen and Speak – Diphthongs /aʊ/ and /əʊ/ (p. 71–72)
Task 1 – now, how, cloud, scout; load, doubt, town, tone: common sound?
/aʊ/ (ಗಮನಿಸಿ: ‘load’ ಮತ್ತು ‘tone’ /əʊ/ ಆಗಿವೆ – ಪುಸ್ತಕದ ದೋಷ)
Task 2 – so, low, boat, coke, close, snow, choke, goal: common sound?
/əʊ/ (the shorter form of /aʊ/)
Reading – ‘Drunken Monkey Kung Fu Scares Village’ (p. 72–73)
1) Where and when was the drunken monkey noticed first?
It was noticed first in Shettykere village (Chikkanayakanahalli) about a month ago.
2) How did addiction affect the monkey? (See paragraph 2)
The monkey became addicted to alcohol, put on weight, ate anything indiscriminately and became aggressive.
3) New words: takes away (P4); Avatar (P5); troubling (P6); monkey (P5); attacking (P3) – give meanings
takes away – snatches; Avatar – incarnation; troubling – harassing, disturbing (P6 ಪಠ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಇಲ್ಲ – ಪುಸ್ತಕ ದೋಷ); monkey – Simian; attacking – aggressive
4) Match the phrases with their meanings: 1) scaring the wits out of 2) getting high 3) wearing thin 4) getting rid of 5) feeling very difficult to do something
1 – making one very afraid; 2 – being overdrunk; 3 – vanishing; 4 – avoiding; 5 – going up the hill (means ‘difficult’)
B. Grammar – The Passive Voice: match and write active and passive sentences (p. 74)
Kalidasa – Shakuntala
Active: Kalidasa wrote Shakuntala. Passive: Shakuntala was written by Kalidasa.
Jayadeva – Geeta Govinda

J.K. Rowling – Harry Potter
Active: J.K. Rowling wrote Harry Potter. Passive: Harry Potter was written by J.K. Rowling.
Galileo – Telescope (e.g.)
Active: Galileo invented the telescope. Passive: The telescope was invented by Galileo.
C. Writing – Complete the story using the outline (p. 74)

Story outline: A cap seller on his way to market ... very hot ... the cool shade of a huge tree ... takes a nap beside his basket of caps ... wakes up ... basket empty ... thinks they are stolen ... noises above ... monkeys with caps on ... desperate efforts to recover the caps ... at last snatches his own cap ... monkeys do the same ... he picks up the caps ... happy.

A cap seller on his way to market felt very hot, so he sat in the cool shade of a huge tree and took a nap beside his basket of caps. When he woke up, he found the basket empty. He thought the caps had been stolen. Then he heard noises above and saw monkeys with caps on their heads. He made desperate efforts to recover the caps, but in vain. At last he snatched his own cap off his head and threw it down. The monkeys did the same, and he picked up the caps and was happy.
C. Writing – Expand one proverb into 5 or 6 sentences (p. 75)
Proverbs: A stitch in time saves nine; Jack of all trades, master of none; Prevention is better than cure; Where there is a will, there is a way; All that glitters is not gold.

Sample (‘Where there is a will, there is a way’): If we really want to achieve something, we can always find a way to do it. A farmer who wants to grow crops in dry land can dig wells and use drip irrigation. A student who wants to pass can make a timetable and study every day. Difficulties may come, but a determined person does not give up. Hence, where there is a will, there is a way. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
POETRY – ILA: Your teacher will recite a poem. Answer (p. 76)
1. Who does ‘I’ refer to in this poem?
‘I’ is the tree itself (the poem ‘Let me live’, L-8A, is read by the teacher).
2. How is the speaker a source of joy to children?
The tree gives shade and branches for children to play, so the children find company and joy under it.
3. Name any two creatures that find comfort from the speaker.
Two creatures: worms (the tree feeds them with tiny figs) and resting herds or shepherds (the tree gives them rest).
4. What do you think will happen to the speaker in the end?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 78)
1. What words in stanzas 1 and 2 mean [a] 100 years and [b] scene?
[a] centuries (‘many centuries’); [b] sight (‘the sight of’)
2. Make a list of all the words used in the poem to describe the ‘axe’.
quick, sharp, glittering, bright (‘bright axe’)
3. Read the words trunk, axe, wood, timber, tree. Which word does not fit into the list?
axe – strike it out (the others are parts or forms of the tree)
C2 – Answer picking the most appropriate options (p. 78)
1. What did the man strike the tree with? [knife, axe, sickle, saw]
axe
2. Who were watching the sight of the man cutting the tree? [women, people, woodcutters, children]
people
3. What did the tree look like? [small, strong, weak, dry]
strong
C3 – Read and discuss with your partner. Then write (p. 78–79)
1. Who do you think ‘I’ refers to in this poem?
‘I’ is the poet himself, an observer who watched the man cutting the tree.
2. Why do you think the poet stopped?
He stopped because he was attracted by the strong, rhythmic movement of the axe and the sight of the man at work.
3. Which line tells us that the tree is aged?
‘How old the tree was’ (stanza 2).
4. Does the poem mean that cutting a tree is a huge loss for human beings? Which line supports your answer?
Yes. ‘But I saw death cut down a thousand men / In that tall lovely legacy of wood’ (stanza 2).
5. Do you think the poet wrote this poem while the tree was being cut? Support your answer.
No. He writes ‘And I remember how I liked the sight’, which shows that he wrote later, remembering the scene.
6. Has the poet made his intention clear to the reader at the end? Which lines support your answer?
Yes. The last lines ‘But I saw death cut down a thousand men / In that tall lovely legacy of wood’ make his view of cutting trees clear.
7. What message does the poem give us?
Trees are valuable to life and should not be cut down carelessly; cutting them causes great harm.
8. What do you learn about trees from this poem?
Trees are old, strong and valuable; they are a lovely legacy that gives life and shelter to many living beings.
9. ‘But I saw death cut down a thousand men.’ Explain. What does the poet mean by ‘lovely legacy of wood’?
Cutting a tree is like killing many living beings, since trees give shelter and life. The ‘lovely legacy of wood’ is the tree as a gift from nature to future generations.
10. Is this poem a sonnet? Check whether it has a rhyme scheme.
It has 14 lines, but it does not have a regular rhyme scheme, so it is not a true sonnet.
Note – Irony: Do you find any expressions of irony in the second stanza?
Yes. ‘Had more good in it than a growing tree’ is said ironically: the speaker does not accept the man’s reasons for cutting the tree, and says the opposite of what he feels.
C4 – Personification (p. 79)
What is personified in the last stanza?
Death is personified (‘death cut down a thousand men’).

lessons.t: Supplementary Reader · Lal Bahadur Shastry – A pen sketch of a great Indian
lessons.words: vitality – vigour, energy; stroll – walk; vendor – seller on the street; facilities – comfort; anxiety – concern; scarcity – non-availability; austere – simple; abolished – did away with, stopped; sole – only, single; associate – additional; tactful – intelligent in handling people; obsequies – rites performed after death; parole – temporary release from prison
lessons.notes: Supplementary Reader lesson 1 of 2 in Part II (numbered n=9 here; the book does not number supplementary lessons). Book spelling: the title and contents use ‘Lal Bahadur Sastry’, while the text uses ‘Shastry’ – the correct spelling is Shastri (ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ). The text gives 'Arialur Railway accident', which is usually spelt 'Ariyalur' – teacher to verify. The book says the Government released him on parole; the line ‘Shastry said, Release me on parole without any conditions’ is in the book. Q.II.2 and II.3 are open-ended; sample points are given.
ab: I. Answer each of the following questions in a sentence or two (p. 85)
1. Why is October 2 a special day in the history of India?
It is the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi (born 1869) and of Lal Bahadur Shastri (born 1904).
2. Where did Lal Bahadur have his education after his studies at school?
He studied at Kashi Vidyapith, Varanasi, for four years.
3. Name at least two positions that Lal Bahadur held as an administrator.
Minister for Home and Transport in Uttar Pradesh; Railway Minister; Home Minister; Prime Minister (any two).
4. Why do you think Lal Bahadur refused to stay at home even during the days of parole?
Because the parole was granted for the sake of his daughter, and she had died; he felt it was not right to stay out of prison, and he kept his word and honesty. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
5. When did Lal Bahadur resign his post as the Railway Minister? What was the reason he gave for this act?
He resigned after the Ariyalur railway accident, accepting moral responsibility for it.
6. How did he respond to Pakistan’s attack?
He declared ‘force will be met with force’, gave the Army freedom to act, and the Indian Army entered Pakistan and won the war.
II. Answer each of the following in a paragraph of 10–12 sentences (p. 85)
1. Give an account of Lal Bahadur’s education.

Lal Bahadur was born on October 2, 1904 at Mughal Sarai. After his school education he went to Varanasi and joined Kashi Vidyapith, where he studied for four years. He was very bright in philosophy, economics, political science and social science. He walked eight miles each way, as he could not afford a bicycle. He was very poor and lived a hard life, spending only two and a half rupees a month. He received the degree ‘Shastry’ while studying there. His hard work and simple living during his education shaped his character. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
2. Narrate any one incident from Lal Bahadur’s life which highlights his honesty.

Lal Bahadur resigned as the Railway Minister after the Ariyalur railway accident, accepting moral responsibility for it. This shows his honesty and sense of duty. Such an act of accepting responsibility made people trust him. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
3. Imagine you are to speak on the life of Lal Bahadur Shastry for 3 minutes. Note down the points.

a) Kindness – gave one anna for fifty mangoes to an old vendor; b) Hard work and education – walked eight miles each way and got the degree ‘Shastry’; c) Honesty and responsibility – resigned after the Ariyalur railway accident; d) Simple living – travelled second class, ate one meal a day, had no car of his own; e) Courage and firmness – ‘force will be met with force’ and the 1965 war. (ಮಾದರಿ ಅಂಶಗಳು)

lessons.t: Supplementary Reader · The First Woman in Space – A saga of an adventurous woman
lessons.au: Edited by Prof. K.B. Prabhuprasad (Supplementary Reader)
lessons.words: credit – honour; cosmonaut – space traveller; thrilling – very joyful; Yuri Gagarin – the first man in space; stamina – strength, guts; humble – simple, not rich; parachute – a device used to descend safely from a height; earnestness – seriousness; rigorous – strict and hard; fulfilment – completion; altitude – height above the earth; landscape – view of land; rigours – hardships; weightlessness – a state in which the body feels no weight; envious – jealous; trade school – a school for learning a skill
lessons.notes: Supplementary Reader lesson 2 of 2 in Part II (numbered n=10 here). Book facts used in answers: Valentina Tereshkova flew in Vostok VI on June 16, 1963. Q.II.2 needs information about Kalpana Chawla which is not in the book; the sample answer uses general knowledge and should be checked by the teacher. Typo to check: 'stood her in good stead' is correct phrasing; the text has ‘Yaroslav’ (Yaroslavl in some sources). Q.II.1 and II.3 are open-ended.
ab: I. Answer each of the following in a sentence or two (p. 88)
1. When did Valentina go round the earth? What was great about this event?
She went round the earth on June 16, 1963. It was great because she was the first woman to travel in space.
2. How did Valentina help her mother? What else was she doing at the same time?
She worked at a tyre factory and then at a textile mill to help her mother maintain the family; at the same time she attended some classes at Yaroslav.
3. How did people all over the world share her joys at the historic moment?
Crowds of people all over the world danced for joy when they heard about her journey.
4. What did she say on landing after the space flight?
She said, ‘It is very nice to be a guest but it is always better at home. When I landed, I felt joy at being at home again.’
5. Apart from flying, what were Valentina’s hobbies?
She was interested in music and literature, and she loved reading. She also sang songs in space.
II. Answer each of the following in a paragraph of about 80–100 words (p. 88)
1. Imagine you are asked to interview Valentina Tereshkova. Prepare a list of questions.

1) How did you feel when you were chosen to fly into space? 2) What inspired you to become a cosmonaut? 3) How did your early life in a village shape your courage? 4) What did you see from space? 5) How did you feel while travelling at high speed? 6) What advice would you give to young women who dream of space? ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
2. Write a paragraph on the similarity and the contrast between the flights of Tereshkova and Kalpana Chawla.

Both Valentina Tereshkova and Kalpana Chawla were brave women who flew into space and made their country proud. Both had a dream and worked hard to achieve it. However, Tereshkova came from a poor family in a Soviet village and flew in 1963 in the Vostok VI, while Kalpana Chawla was born in India, studied abroad and flew on the American space shuttle Columbia in 1997 and 2003. Tereshkova was the first woman in space, whereas Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Indian origin to fly in space. (ಪುಸ್ತಕದಲ್ಲಿ ಇಲ್ಲದ ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯ ಮಾಹಿತಿ)
3. What do you think youngsters like you can learn from the life of Valentina Tereshkova? Discuss and write.

Youngsters can learn that a poor background is not a barrier to success, that hard work, courage and determination help one achieve big dreams, and that one should be humble and keep a love for home and learning. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

lessons.t: Listening Passages · L-1 to L-8A (ಆಲಿಕೆ ಪಠ್ಯ)
lessons.words: book-worms – students who only memorise; parole – temporary release from prison; flaming – burning brightly; frozen – very cold; compliments – words of praise; horns – hard pointed growths on the head; barber – a person who cuts hair; ashamed – feeling guilty or embarrassed; hypnotize – to put a person in a trance; helpless – unable to do anything; shady – giving shade; herds – groups of animals; shepherds – people who look after sheep or goats
lessons.notes: Listening passages L-1 to L-8A are read aloud by the teacher; the book prints no questions for them. Answers below are the teacher’s sample questions. Passage links: L-1 is the Unit 1 story of Sangappa (Sem-1 text), L-5 is the Unit 5 ILA, L-6 is the Unit 6 ILA, L-7 is the Unit 7 ILA, L-8 is the Unit 8 ILA. L-2 about Bhaskara II and L-8A are poems/passages for listening only. Book spelling: ‘Bhaskara’ is printed correctly; ‘Kalachakra’ is the book’s term.
ab: Listening Passages – teacher reads aloud, then asks (p. 89–92)
L-1 (Sangappa at the Ashram): Why did Sangappa feel sad?
He expected his son to be studying in a class, but he found there were no classes and his son was sitting under a tree watching birds.
L-2 (Bhaskara II): Who was Bhaskara II, and where was he born?
He was a famous scientist and a great poet, a Kannadiga born in Vijayapura. He invented Kalachakra, the time-clock.
L-3 (Gandhiji in South Africa): Why was Gandhiji thrown out of the train?
He had a first class ticket and refused to move to another compartment; two policemen forcefully pushed him out of the train.
L-4 (The little match girl): Why did the girl not want to go home?
Her father would beat her for not bringing back any money from selling matches.
L-5 (Two women and the baby): Who did the minister give the baby to, and why?
To the second woman, because she did not want the baby to be divided, which showed that she was the real mother.
L-6 (Qualities of people): Name one desirable and one undesirable quality mentioned.
Desirable: Kamala is friendly and polite. Undesirable: Maya is always late to school.
L-7 (The king with horns): Why did the king get horns on his head?
Because he boasted that he was more attractive than the gods, and the gods wanted to teach him a lesson.
L-8 (Magician Jadoogar Goga): What tricks did the magician say he can perform?
He can make a lunch box disappear within a second and change a piece of paper into a hundred rupee note.
L-8A (Let Me Live – poem): What does the tree give to people and animals?
Shade, tiny figs to feed worms, homes for tiny creatures, resting place for herds and shepherds, and the air people breathe.
